title: Behavioral Detection of Command History Clearing
shortTitle: Behavioral Detection of Command History Clearing
summary: This strategy detects the clearing of command history, where an operator erases the record of what was typed in a shell or console so that later investigation cannot reconstruct their steps. The covered technique matters because command history is often the only readable narrative of what an intruder did on a host, and it is frequently the difference between understanding an incident and guessing at it. Shell process execution logs, console history file telemetry and file deletion events make it possible, because the deletion or truncation of a history file is recorded separately from the shell that created it. The main failure mode is that automation, cleanup scripts and privacy tooling delete the same files routinely, so the rule must weigh who deleted the file, which host it happened on and whether a shell session was active at that moment.

beginner.definition: This detection watches for a user or program wiping the list of commands typed in a terminal. That list is stored in a small file on disk. Removing it erases the story of what happened on the machine.
beginner.whyItMatters: Command history shows the steps an intruder took, including which tools they ran and what they looked at. When it is erased, the investigation loses its timeline and may miss other systems involved. Legitimate administrators almost never need to erase it. On Windows, clearing an event log is an even louder version of the same idea.
howItWorks: Each shell writes the commands you type into a history file in your home folder.
The endpoint records when that file is deleted, truncated or replaced.
The detection also watches for commands that clear history while the shell runs.
On Windows it watches for the audit log clearing event, which records who cleared a log.
It then checks whether a shell session was open under the same account at that time.
A match raises an alert because erasing records is itself suspicious.
beginner.example: Imagine a visitor sign in sheet at an office. An intruder walks past reception, tears out the page with their name on it, and leaves. The torn page tells you more than the remaining pages ever could, because only one person needed that page gone.
takeaways: The act of erasing history is often more suspicious than the commands that were erased.
Watch both the history file and the log clearing event, on Linux and Windows.
A single history wipe after a long interactive session deserves immediate attention.

objectives: Name the files and events that hold command history on Linux, macOS and Windows.
Detect deletion, truncation and in memory clearing of shell history.
Interpret the Windows audit log cleared event and identify the account responsible.
Correlate a history wipe with an active shell session on the same host and account.
Explain how history loss changes the scope of an incident investigation.
dataSources: Linux auditd file watch records for unlink, rename and truncate operations on shell history files in user home directories
Linux auditd execve records showing shell history clearing commands and their arguments
Windows Security event 1102 recording that the audit log was cleared, with the subject account and logon identifier
Sysmon event 23 file delete records, or equivalent file system delete telemetry, for the PowerShell console history file in user and administrator profiles
PowerShell script block and module logging capturing history clearing cmdlets and their invoking session
logic: The pattern is the destruction of a record keeping artifact rather than the destruction of an operational file. The telemetry is the auditd file watch on shell history paths, the execve records for the shell session, the Windows audit log cleared event and the console history file delete record, and the fields that must be correlated are the file path, the operation type, the acting account, the process that performed the deletion, the host name and the presence of an interactive shell session from the same account in the same window. Benign behaviour is a provisioning or golden image script that cleans a template profile, a privacy tool that removes a departing employee's shell history, or an administrator rotating logs as part of an approved maintenance task, all of which usually run as automation from a management account rather than from an interactive session. Malicious behaviour is the deletion of one user's history file moments after a long interactive session, a shell command that unsets the history file for the current session, or an audit log cleared event on a host where the log had recently recorded unusual activity. The combination of the deletion and the interactive session is the discriminator, because automation cleans up without typing.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Interactive shell history file cleared by the session owner
# logsource:
#   product: linux
#   service: auditd
# detection:
#   selection:
#     type: SYSCALL
#     syscall:
#       - unlink
#       - unlinkat
#       - truncate
#     key: shell_history_watch
#   filter_provisioning:
#     exe:
#       - '/usr/bin/cloud-init'
#       - '/usr/sbin/userdel'
#   condition: selection and not filter_provisioning
# level: medium
falsePositives: Provisioning and golden image pipelines that reset a template user profile and remove example history files
Departed employee offboarding automation that deletes the home directory contents including shell history
Privacy or hardening scripts that are approved to remove command history from shared jump hosts on a schedule
Log rotation or retention jobs that archive and then delete history files under a change record
Backup or configuration management agents that truncate files they are templating, including history stubs in profiles
tuningNotes: First record which accounts and processes are allowed to delete files under home directories, then exclude the automation and offboarding identities and keep the rule at high severity for interactive accounts. Add the full path pattern for each shell history file your estate uses and scope the highest severity to server and domain controller groups, where interactive shell use is rare. On Windows, treat the audit log cleared event as always alertable and separate it from the console history file case, because the two carry different meanings. The coverage you lose by excluding automation accounts is genuine destruction performed through a compromised service account, so alert whenever an automation identity deletes a history file outside its scheduled window, and keep a weekly report of history wipes alongside log clearing events for trend review.
